item.content:encoded: Overall, a well constructed article. My question is why, after discovering the anti-electronic and absorption of human aspect, was a fully mechanical option sent in? A steam, or internal combustion powered vehicle, with an analog video camera, could easily be programed with a clockwork, or punchcard path. In case 'something' fogs the fim, useing a long fiber optic cable with oil lamps for spotlights would a lot for real-time observations. The programming of a path is particularly easy, since exact measurements can be taken during the SCiPs inactive phase. It just seems like a logical progression for the Foundation to make.

item.content:encoded: I liked this and voted accordingly. One minor nitpick, though: I don't think they'd have gone in carrying an unloaded weapon, even for a quick "peek-and-grab" mission. Much more likely that they'd be armed but not readied. That way, if suddenly attacked it's just a matter of cocking and firing. If they don't have a magazine in, they have to grab one, load it in, THEN cock it. Two or three seconds can make an awfully big difference :)

item.content:encoded: The reasoning, really, was that the initial team was just a "peek" team of undercover agents looking for incriminating documents or mostly mundane objects. Lightly armed and not carrying their full equipment, they probably weren't equipped to deal with severe paranormal activity. Hence the call for backup.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
They could just be a little paranoid given the average life expectancy of retrieval teams around here, but that's a little meta for this one page. As a standalone it does seem odd that they'd pull an armed team out at the first sniff of weirdness—if they were expecting the possibility of losing a whole team so suddenly they'd not send in a bunch of armed men to begin with.

Like Photo said above, it's the way the team's equipment was retrieved that really puts this over the top.
